analysis.one_liner: Repeals workplace safety inspections, citations, and penalties while adding small-business safety help.
analysis.headline: A single Republican congressman's bill to strip OSHA of its inspection, citation, and penalty powers died in a House subcommittee without a single cosponsor or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have repealed the sections of the 1970 workplace safety law that let federal inspectors examine workplaces, cite violations, and impose fines and criminal penalties. It would have replaced the existing rule-writing standard with a strict cost-benefit test, and it would have legalized employer-run employee safety committees under federal labor law. It also created a small-business safety assistance program funded with at least a quarter of OSHA's budget, and an award program for safe companies.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers, especially those in hazardous industries, would gain the most: the bill repeals OSHA's inspection, citation, enforcement, and penalty provisions, and imposes a cost-benefit test on any new safety standard. Small businesses would also gain from the new consultation and training program. Non-union employers would gain from legalized employee participation committees.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the sections of the Occupational Safety and Health Act covering inspections, investigations, recordkeeping, citations, enforcement, judicial review, and civil and criminal penalties [S2][S3].

It requires a continuing economic analysis of the costs and benefits of each OSHA standard and adds cost-benefit findings as a condition for new standards, including that a standard minimize employment loss in affected industries [S2][S3].

It creates a small business assistance and training program of technical and consultative services, targeted at small employers and the most hazardous industries, and requires that at least one-fourth of OSHA's annual appropriation go to this program [S2][S3].

It provides that employee safety and health participation committees are not 'labor organizations' under the National Labor Relations Act or the Railway Labor Act, legalizing such committees even where workers are not unionized [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers in dangerous jobs would bear the cost: the bill removes the federal inspection, citation, and penalty machinery that gives safety standards any teeth. Unionized workers would also lose, because employer-run committees that do not bargain collectively would no longer be restricted under federal labor law.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the inspection, citation, and penalty provisions would leave safety standards without their main enforcement mechanism; the CRS summary lists inspections, citations, enforcement, and penalties among the repealed provisions [S2].
A cost-benefit requirement, including a duty to minimize employment loss in affected industries, would slow or block standards that protect workers when compliance costs are high [S3].
Legalizing employee participation committees outside collective bargaining could give employers a compliant employee body on safety matters without independent union representation [S3].
Dedicating at least one-fourth of OSHA's annual appropriation to the assistance program would shrink the share of the budget available for inspections and enforcement [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The small-business consultation program and the safety award are reasonable ideas that already resemble parts of OSHA's voluntary programs. But they sit on top of a bill whose core effect is to repeal inspections, citations, enforcement, and penalties — the tools that make safety rules real. On balance, the bill's value flows overwhelmingly to employers, and its cost falls on workers who rely on federal inspections to keep their workplaces safe.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with no cosponsors, referred to committee and then to a subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended two months later, never reaching a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Joel Hefley introduced the bill in the House on September 30, 1994, near the end of the two-year Congress [S1][S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor, and on October 26, 1994 to its Subcommittee on Labor Standards, Occupational Health and Safety [S5].
No further action was taken before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995, so the bill died without a floor vote [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary workers came out ahead: the inspection, citation, and penalty provisions of federal workplace safety law stayed intact. The bill's lone sponsor and the employers who would have been relieved of federal enforcement lost an opportunity they never got to vote on.

for.name: Rep. Joel Hefley
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor; introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the House floor.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee and never reported it back for a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, and never advanced far enough for any vote to reveal a partisan split [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill repeals inspections, citations, enforcement, and civil and criminal penalties, and makes new standards pass a cost-benefit test. The relief to employers comes directly out of the enforcement that protects workers.

A dedicated assistance and training program, funded with at least a quarter of OSHA's budget, would give small employers free consultative services on compliance. This is a genuine benefit, though it is paired with the repeal of enforcement.

Legalizing employee participation committees that do not bargain collectively would let employers set up worker bodies on safety outside union structures. Union members would keep OSHA protections the bill leaves standing, but the union role in safety would be weakened where such committees replace it.
